No slides were found for this lecture. The page is built from the doctor's notes (green) and every gift (red). Aldughaither's summaries have no liver-mass chapter.

Surgical anatomy

  • Couinaud segments I–VIII — each segment needs all four: portal venous inflow, hepatic arterial inflow, hepatic venous outflow, biliary drainage (same principle for transplant grafts).
  • Pringle manoeuvre: clamp the portal vein + hepatic artery (hepatoduodenal ligament) → stops inflow. Bleeding despite Pringle → hepatic veins/IVC (retrograde).
  • Structure not in the portal triad → hepatic vein (triad = portal vein, hepatic artery, bile duct). 438 ×2
  • Functional reserve matters, not volume: a healthy liver tolerates ~70% resection; a cirrhotic liver may fail after a small resection; decompensated cirrhosis → no resection.

Benign liver masses

HaemangiomaFNHHepatic adenoma
NatureMost common benign tumour (~5%), vascularHyperplasia of normal hepatocytesPremalignant, OCP/hormone-related
Key imagingPeripheral nodular enhancement → centripetal fill-in → delayed complete filling; T2 very brightCentral stellate scar with radiating spokesMay mimic early HCC
Malignant potentialNoneNone→ HCC; rupture/haemorrhage
BiopsyAvoid (bleeding, non-diagnostic)Unnecessary (shows normal liver)—
ManagementObserveNo treatmentStop OCP → observe ≤ 1 year → persistent → surgery
  • Haemangioma work-up: US → multiphasic CT → MRI if doubtful. Surgery only for symptoms (subcapsular lesion stretching Glisson's capsule — the parenchyma itself has little pain sensation), progressive enlargement, or mass effect.
  • OSCE pattern: young woman, persistent RUQ pain, liver lesion → multiphasic CT → peripheral enhancement → centripetal filling → haemangioma.
  • Peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in → haemangioma. 442
  • Hypervascular lesion with a central stellate scar → FNH 442; incidental 3-cm FNH → no treatment needed. 438 ×2
  • OCP user, incidental arterially enhancing mass → stop OCPs, repeat imaging in 6 months 441; adenoma not regressing 6 months after stopping OCP → surgical resection. 442 ×3

Liver cysts & abscesses

  • Simple cyst, multiple simple cysts, polycystic disease, biliary cyst, hydatid cyst.
  • Simple cyst: serous; large/subcapsular → pain. Needle aspiration is not definitive (re-accumulates, infection → abscess). Laparoscopic deroofing/fenestration is preferred. Treat only cysts that truly cause symptoms.
  • "All are liver cysts except" → metastasis (from colon cancer is solid). 426
  • Cyst that can look like a solid mass on CT → hydatid cyst (degenerated/calcified type). 438
  • Most serious complication of hepatic hydatid disease → anaphylaxis (rupture/spillage). 429
  • Amoebic liver abscess (positive E. histolytica serology) → initial antiamoebic drugs (metronidazole). 429 ×2
  • Pyogenic liver abscess with Streptococcus faecalis (gut organism) → spread via the portal route. 426

Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)

  • Primary malignant tumours: HCC, cholangiocarcinoma, fibrolamellar (HCC variant in the young).
  • Background: chronic liver disease/cirrhosis — a "fertile field" that can produce new HCC even after resection. Risk factors: viral hepatitis, alcohol, metabolic disease, iron and copper storage disorders. HBV can cause HCC without cirrhosis.
  • Weakest association with HCC (smoker on HRT with HBV + HCV) → OCP/hormones 436; all predispose except → keyed smoking (least risk; hepatitis A causes no chronic disease). 426
  • Egyptian man with bilharziasis → HCC risk (schistosomiasis + HCV co-infection). 427 ×2
  • Paraneoplastic syndromes of HCC — all except → keyed hyperglycaemia (HCC causes hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, erythrocytosis). 426
  • Spread: local satellites, venous tumour thrombus, lung (hepatic veins → IVC → heart → lungs), bone (vertebrae), brain.
  • AFP raised in ~70% (30% negative) — useful for follow-up only if raised at baseline.
  • HBV cirrhosis, jaundice and weight loss, hypervascular mass → confirm with α-fetoprotein. 426
  • Diagnosis: US → multiphasic (triphasic) CT → MRI if equivocal.
Classic HCC (cirrhotic liver): arterial-phase hyperenhancement + washout in the portal/delayed phase — in the same lesion. No biopsy needed in a cirrhotic with classic imaging (biopsy if non-cirrhotic or atypical).
  • HCV cirrhosis, 2-cm lesion with early arterial enhancement and early washout → HCC. 439 ×5
  • Worse prognosis: larger, multiple, bilobar, extrahepatic spread, cirrhosis, poor performance status, aggressive biology, vascular invasion.

Treatment — tumour burden + liver function

Milan criteria → transplant: single tumour < 5 cm, or ≤ 3 tumours each < 3 cm (extended: solitary up to ~6.5 cm without vascular/nodal/extrahepatic disease). Bridge with locoregional therapy while waiting.
  • 4-cm HCC with Child B cirrhosis → liver transplant. 438 ×5
  • Resection: good when liver function is preserved and the patient is fit (keeps native liver, no immunosuppression); decompensated → poor candidate.

  • Response = no enhancement on contrast CT (not size).
  • Gross: haemangioma spongy; HCC soft, may necrose/rupture; cholangiocarcinoma very hard with capsular retraction.

Cholangiocarcinoma, Caroli disease & TIPS

  • Cholangiocarcinoma: malignant biliary epithelium; intrahepatic lesions hard with capsular retraction.
  • Cholangiocarcinoma is most common at the bifurcation of the hepatic ducts (Klatskin tumour). 426
  • Choledochal cysts types I–V; type V = Caroli disease → intrahepatic strictures + dilatations → stasis → stones → cholangiocarcinoma.
  • TIPS — portal vein ↔ hepatic vein stent to lower portal pressure (variceal bleeding); removed with the liver at transplant.
